NEW DELHI- India stepped up its efforts to expand global maritime partnerships on the second day of Sagarmanthan: The Great Oceans Dialogue 2026, with Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal holding bilateral talks with Saudi Arabia, Belgium and Bhutan on port investment, green shipping, regional connectivity and maritime skills.
The most significant development was Saudi Arabia’s expressed interest in investing in Indian port projects and the Maritime Development Fund (MDF). Discussions between Sonowal and a delegation from the Saudi Ports Authority, Mawani, covered possible Saudi participation in projects including Vadhavan and Galathea Bay, along with cooperation in shipbuilding, seafarer training and resilient supply chains.
The discussions reflect India’s broader effort to attract international investment and strengthen its maritime infrastructure while developing a more resilient shipping and supply-chain ecosystem.

Push for green shipping with Belgium
In talks with Annick De Ridder, Flemish Minister for Mobility, Public Works, Ports and Sport, Sonowal proposed exploring a green shipping corridor between Indian ports and Antwerp-Bruges.
The discussions covered green fuels, smart-port technologies and dredging. VOC Port and the Port of Antwerp have also signed an agreement focusing on capacity building in green shipping and green fuel.
The proposed corridor aligns with India’s efforts to expand cleaner maritime transport and develop ports capable of supporting alternative green fuels.
Also Read- Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi, Among 250 Others Detained in New Delhi
India also discussed strengthening maritime connectivity with Bhutan, with Sonowal highlighting National Waterway-2 and the Jogighopa terminal as potential gateways for Bhutanese trade to global markets.
The two sides discussed the potential of the Manas and Sankosh rivers and their connectivity with India’s national waterways to improve cargo movement. They also discussed maritime training opportunities for Bhutanese youth at the Centre of Excellence in Dibrugarh, which is under development.
The Bhutan discussions are particularly relevant to India’s efforts to use inland waterways and multimodal connectivity to link the Northeast more closely with regional and international trade networks.
Sonowal said the discussions with Saudi Arabia, Belgium and Bhutan demonstrated the expanding geographical reach of India’s maritime partnerships, covering investment, green shipping, waterways and skills development.
Also Read- Gyanesh Kumar Under Protest Spotlight: CJP Rally in Mumbai, Student Agitation in Delhi
Youth and women at centre of maritime strategy
Beyond international partnerships, Day 2 of Sagarmanthan placed considerable emphasis on young people and women in India’s maritime sector.
At sessions titled “The Future is Blue: The Next Maritime Generation” and “Ocean Changemakers: Women, Youth and India’s Maritime Journey,” Sonowal heard from young Indians and women about their aspirations for the sector. An all-women tri-service sailing expedition also participated in the programme.
According to the ministry, the number of Indian seafarers has increased from 1.27 lakh to 3.23 lakh over the past 12 years, taking India from fifth place in 2015 to the world’s second-largest supplier of seafarers, with more than 12 per cent of the global workforce.
The number of active women seafarers has also increased from 1,599 in 2021 to 7,033 in 2025. The government aims to further increase women’s participation through its Mission 20% by 2030 initiative.
Sonowal said India’s maritime future would be shaped by its youth and highlighted efforts to expand skills, institutions and career opportunities in the sector.
India expands maritime engagement across regions
Day 2 also saw Minister of State for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Shantanu Thakur hold bilateral discussions with Greece, Lithuania, Mozambique and Myanmar.
The talks covered maritime cooperation, direct shipping links, green ports, shipbuilding, ship repair, seafarer training, the next phase of Sittwe Port, cross-border inland water trade and maritime safety in the Bay of Bengal.
Addressing a press conference, Sonowal highlighted the growth of India’s maritime infrastructure over the past 12 years. According to figures presented by the ministry, port capacity increased from 1,561 MTPA to 2,817 MTPA, while cargo handled increased from 1,052 million tonnes to 1,668 million tonnes. Inland waterways cargo rose from 29 million tonnes to 218 million tonnes, while median container vessel turnaround time fell from 35 hours to 23 hours.
Sagarmanthan has also expanded its international participation, with more than 70 countries represented in the 2026 edition, including 10 visiting ministers, according to the ministry.
Sonowal said India was seeking to translate the dialogue into joint research, investment and technology partnerships, particularly in green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol, with the aim of developing Indian ports as green-fuel bunkering hubs.
The broader objective, he said, is to build partnerships for safer seas, greener shipping and shared prosperity.

articles.title: 'Melonellum': Italy's parliament gives final approval to PM Meloni's electoral reform - The New Indian Express
articles.summary: 'Melonellum': Italy's parliament gives final approval to PM Meloni's electoral reform  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
ROME: Italy's parliament gave final approval on Thursday to a sweeping overhaul of the country's electoral system, handing Premier Giorgia Meloni a key political victory while setting up a likely constitutional battle over the reform.
The proposal — dubbed by supporters and critics alike the "Stabilicum" or "Melonellum" — is widely viewed as an attempt to strengthen Italy's political system while improving the electoral prospects of the center-right coalition led by Meloni, which last month celebrated its record as Italy's longest-serving government since WWII.
Supporters say the law is designed to produce clearer election winners and more stable governments in a country known for frequent changes of administration. But the center-left opposition dubbed it "scam law," arguing the reform is unconstitutional. It has pledged to challenge it and bring it in front of Italy's Constitutional Court once it takes effect.
The Chamber of Deputies approved the measure in a secret ballot by 227 votes to 164, giving definitive parliamentary approval to the legislation after months of heated debate.
The reform introduces a big majority prize that will award bonus parliamentary seats in both houses of parliament to the winning pre-election alliance, provided it wins at least 42% of the national vote.
Critics contend that such a "majority prize" distorts voter representation and could conflict with previous court rulings that struck down elements of earlier electoral laws. A successful challenge could force Meloni's conservative government to revise the system before the next general election.
The new law abolishes Italy's current mixed electoral system, in which about one-third of parliamentary seats are elected in first-past-the-post constituencies, and replaces it with a fully proportional system.
Meloni's coalition says the changes will make it easier for voters to identify a governing coalition before elections and reduce the post-election bargaining that has often produced fragile governments. To qualify for the majority prize, parties will have to agree on a common prime ministerial candidate and political platform before the election.
The reform puts additional pressure on the divided center-left opposition, where tensions between the Democratic Party and the populist Five-Star Movement have complicated efforts to build a unified alliance capable of challenging the government in next year's election.
Meloni had made the vote on the electoral law a test of coalition unity, warning lawmakers from her Brothers of Italy party and coalition partners Forza Italia and the League that the government could face a crisis if the reform were defeated.
Yet resistance to the law has emerged within Meloni's own coalition.
Some lawmakers fear the measure could ultimately backfire as support for former general Roberto Vannacci's nationalist National Future party threatens to siphon votes from the governing bloc, potentially making it harder for it to reach the 42% threshold required to secure the majority bonus.
Others have criticized provisions they say would increase campaign costs for individual candidates and reduce women's representation in parliament.
The vote marks Meloni's latest attempt to reshape Italy's institutional framework after voters earlier this year rejected her proposed overhaul of the justice system in a constitutional referendum.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi marked 25 consecutive years as a head of government on 7 October 2026, a milestone spanning his tenure as Chief Minister of Gujarat and his leadership of India since 2014. The anniversary offers an opportunity to examine his political career, India’s economic development, its growing international role and the expanding relationship between India and Hungary.
Narendra Modi began his journey as a head of government on 7 October 2001, when he took office as Chief Minister of Gujarat, one of India’s most economically important states. Almost thirteen years later, he became Prime Minister of India following the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) victory in the 2014 general election.
Modi subsequently secured second and third terms as Prime Minister following the elections in 2019 and 2024, making him one of the country’s longest-serving national leaders.
The 25-year anniversary was marked by the Indian government, while several world leaders sent messages of congratulations recognising the milestone.
Over this period, India has experienced considerable economic and technological change, alongside an increasingly prominent position in international diplomacy.
From Gujarat to New Delhi: A quarter-century in government
Modi assumed office in Gujarat at a challenging time. The state was recovering from a devastating earthquake earlier in 2001, and reconstruction, infrastructure development and economic recovery were among the government’s immediate priorities.
During his tenure, Gujarat pursued industrial development, investment promotion and improvements to transport and energy infrastructure.
The Vibrant Gujarat investment summit, launched in 2003, became an important platform for attracting domestic and international businesses to the state.
In 2014, Modi moved from state to national politics after the BJP won a parliamentary majority in India’s general election. He was sworn in as Prime Minister on 26 May that year.
His government’s priorities have subsequently included industrial development, digitalisation, infrastructure investment, financial inclusion and expanding India’s international economic partnerships.
India’s economic development and digital transformation
India has strengthened its position among the world’s largest economies over the past decade, supported by domestic consumption, investment and the expansion of its services and technology sectors.
One of the Modi government’s flagship economic initiatives is Make in India, launched in September 2014 to encourage manufacturing, attract foreign investment and strengthen the country’s participation in global supply chains.
Another major programme, Digital India, introduced in 2015, focuses on expanding digital infrastructure, improving access to online public services and encouraging technology adoption throughout the country.
India‘s Unified Payments Interface (UPI), a digital payment system launched in 2016, has become an important part of everyday financial transactions, allowing users to transfer money directly between bank accounts through mobile applications.
Infrastructure development has also remained a major government priority. Investments in motorways, railways, airports, ports and logistics networks are intended to improve connectivity and support economic activity across the country.
Meanwhile, India’s pharmaceutical, information technology, telecommunications and automotive industries continue to play significant roles in its economy.
The government’s longer-term development strategy is centred on Viksit Bharat 2047, an initiative aimed at transforming India into a developed country by 2047, the centenary of its independence.
India’s expanding role in international affairs
India’s international profile has grown considerably during Modi’s premiership.
The country has strengthened its engagement with major economic and political partners, including the European Union, the United States, Japan and countries across the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia.
India also maintains important relationships with Russia and participates in multilateral organisations such as the G20, BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.
In 2023, New Delhi hosted the G20 Leaders’ Summit under India’s presidency, bringing together representatives of the world’s leading economies.
The summit addressed issues including global economic development, sustainable growth, financial cooperation and the interests of developing economies.
India’s approach to international relations continues to emphasise strategic autonomy, allowing New Delhi to pursue partnerships with different countries while maintaining its own foreign policy priorities.
As the world’s most populous country and a major emerging economy, India is expected to remain an important participant in discussions concerning international trade, technology, energy security and global governance.
EU–India free trade agreement: A major milestone in economic relations
One of the most significant recent developments in India’s international economic relations came on 27 January 2026, when the European Union and India concluded negotiations on a landmark Free Trade Agreement (FTA).
The agreement followed nearly two decades of negotiations and represents a major step towards closer economic cooperation between two of the world’s largest markets.
Together, the EU and India account for approximately two billion people, creating considerable opportunities for businesses, investors and exporters.
The agreement is designed to reduce tariffs, remove trade barriers and improve market access for companies operating in both economies.
According to the European Commission, the deal will eliminate or reduce tariffs on more than 96% of EU goods exports to India. It is also expected to support investment, strengthen supply chains and encourage further commercial cooperation.
The potential benefits extend to several sectors, including automotive manufacturing, machinery, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and other industrial products.
For Hungary, the agreement could create additional opportunities for exporters and manufacturers seeking access to the expanding Indian market.
Hungarian companies operating in automotive components, industrial machinery, pharmaceuticals and advanced technologies could benefit from improved trading conditions once the agreement takes effect.
The EU–India agreement is not yet in force. Following the conclusion of negotiations in January, the European Commission submitted proposals for its signature and conclusion to the Council of the European Union in September 2026. The necessary approval procedures must be completed before the agreement can be implemented.
Nevertheless, the conclusion of negotiations already represents an important development in relations between India and Europe, with potential long-term implications for Hungary’s trade and investment ties.
Hungary and India: Strengthening bilateral relations
India’s growing economic significance has also created new opportunities for cooperation with Hungary.
The two countries maintain longstanding diplomatic relations, with cooperation spanning trade, investment, education, science and culture.
According to figures published by the Embassy of India in Budapest, bilateral trade reached approximately USD 2.4 billion in 2025, compared with around USD 1.3 billion in 2024.
Indian investment in Hungary amounts to approximately USD 3.3 billion, underlining the importance of bilateral business relations.
Indian companies have established operations in Hungary across several sectors, while Hungarian businesses are also exploring opportunities in the Indian market.
Machinery, electrical equipment, pharmaceuticals, chemicals and automotive products feature among the major categories of goods traded between the two countries.
Diplomatic engagement remains an important part of this relationship. As we wrote in September, India and Hungary strengthen ties as foreign ministers meet in NY.
His Excellency Anshuman Gaur, the current Ambassador of India to Hungary, assumed his post in Budapest in 2025. The growing importance of EU–India economic relations has also featured in diplomatic and business discussions in Budapest. In February 2026, the Embassy of India organised a business seminar entitled New Economic Horizon: The India–EU FTA and the Union Budget 2026 – Opportunities for Hungary. The event brought together representatives of the Hungarian and Indian business communities, policymakers and other stakeholders to discuss the implications of the free trade agreement. Ambassador Gaur addressed the significance of the agreement and the opportunities it could create for Hungarian and Indian enterprises.
Beyond economic relations, educational and cultural exchanges continue to contribute to closer ties between the two countries.
Indian students attend Hungarian universities, including through international scholarship programmes, while cultural cooperation encompasses literature, music, academic research and other fields.
Looking ahead: India’s development ambitions
Narendra Modi’s 25 years as a head of government coincide with a period of substantial change in India’s economy, infrastructure and international engagement.
From his early years as Chief Minister of Gujarat to his third term as India’s Prime Minister, his political career has been closely associated with programmes aimed at modernising the country and expanding its economic opportunities.
The Indian government’s Viksit Bharat 2047 initiative provides a longer-term framework for its development ambitions, focusing on economic growth, technological progress, infrastructure and social development.
At the international level, India’s partnerships with the European Union and individual European countries are likely to remain important components of its economic strategy.

Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi today inaugurated the 10th edition of India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026, Asia’s leading digital technology and telecommunications forum, at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi. The event brings together policymakers, global technology leaders, telecom operators, innovators, startups, investors, academia and international stakeholders to shape the future of digital connectivity and emerging technologies.
The event is being organised jointly by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), Ministry of Communications, and the Cellular Operators Association of India (COAI) under the overarching theme “Scale Without Boundaries”, reflecting India’s ambition to take digital innovation, connectivity and technology-led growth beyond traditional boundaries.
Union Minister for Communications and Development of North Eastern Region Shri Jyotiraditya M. Scindia and Minister of State for Communications and Rural Development Dr. Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani were among the dignitaries present on the occasion.
Addressing the gathering, Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi emphasised the transformative role of technology and the importance of innovation, connectivity and digital solutions in driving inclusive and sustainable development.
The Prime Minister also said “I would like to thank and welcome all the representatives of telecom operators, industrial leaders, experts, academia or startups all across the world to India. India Mobile Congress is the testament of India’s evolving telecom sector and digital connectivity. In 2022, we launched 5G from this platform. In 2023, I explained how India transformed from 5G rollout to 5G reachout and today, we are witnessing how 5G has reached every district of our country. Today, India has 5,50,000 5G Base Stations and mobile internet speed from 2022, has increased by 10 times. The revolution that has taken place in the telecom sector has directly benefited the citizens of India. Today, hundreds of government services are available through mobile phones. Government assistance is now reaching beneficiaries directly through their bank accounts. Through Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT), nearly ₹50 lakh crore has been transferred directly to beneficiaries and credited to their bank accounts. This is not a small figure. It has also helped prevent nearly ₹5 lakh crore from reaching the wrong hands.”
The Prime Minister emphasized “Over the years, India has transformed from being a consumer to a creator. Now, the country is moving towards a stage where product design will also take place in India. The technology and intellectual property (IP) behind these products will also be Indian. All necessary incentives are being provided, and all essential reforms are being implemented to achieve this. In short, the 'Reform Express' is speeding ahead in the telecom sector as well.”

Shri Scindia said, “The decade-long journey of the India Mobile Congress serves as the table of contents for India's digital transformation story. When IMC was launched in 2017 with the theme 'Connecting the Next Billion,' the nation faced an immense challenge. Today, we have built a thriving ecosystem with over 1.35 billion telecom subscribers and more than 1.09 billion broadband connections. 10 years ago, 0.26 GB was the average Indian’s monthly data consumption. Highlighting the journey of last 12 years, Shri Scindia said “One GB of data would cost Rs. 268 in 2014. Today, twelve years later, one GB of data costs only eight rupees.”

The 10th edition of IMC marks a significant milestone in India's journey towards becoming a global hub for telecommunications, digital innovation and technology development.
With the theme “Scale Without Boundaries,” IMC 2026 focuses on taking innovations from laboratories and pilot projects to widespread deployment and real-world applications. The theme reflects India's vision of building a digitally empowered, secure and growth-oriented ecosystem where technology can reach every sector, region and community.
The four key pillars of IMC 2026
Srishti – Building the Future: Promoting innovation, emerging technologies and next-generation digital infrastructure.
Samvardhan – Fueling Growth: Accelerating investment, entrepreneurship, manufacturing and industry-led growth.
Sashakt – Expanding Opportunities: Leveraging digital technologies to create opportunities for citizens, enterprises and communities.
Suraksha – Strengthening Trust: Building secure, resilient and trusted digital networks and technology ecosystems.

The Union Minister also interacted with participating innovators and industry representatives, encouraging continued collaboration between government, industry, startups and research institutions to accelerate the development and deployment of indigenous technologies.

The DoT pavilion also provides visitors and international delegates an opportunity to understand India's policy initiatives, technology development programmes and institutional efforts aimed at building a resilient and future-ready telecom ecosystem.

The launches demonstrate the increasing maturity of India's indigenous technology ecosystem and the potential of Indian companies and innovators to develop solutions for both domestic and international markets.
The Government's continued emphasis on research, innovation, product development, manufacturing and global partnerships is aimed at strengthening India's position in the global telecommunications value chain.

A US delegation is expected to arrive in Israel in coming days to assess whether the country is meeting the security conditions of the US Visa Waiver Program.
Israelis could lose their visa-free access to the United States after security lapses reportedly came to light following the thwarted attack on a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight.
A US delegation is expected to arrive in Israel in the coming days to assess whether the country is meeting the security conditions of the US Visa Waiver Program, The Times of Israel reported, citing Channel 12. The delegation is currently in the United Arab Emirates, where it is reviewing aviation security procedures, according to the report.
Israel became part of the US Visa Waiver Program in 2023. Under the arrangement, Israeli citizens can travel to the US using an Electronic System for Travel Authorization (ESTA) instead of going through the longer visa application process. The upcoming review will examine whether Israel continues to meet the requirements agreed when it joined the programme.
The scrutiny follows the September 30 incident involving flydubai Flight 1073, in which copilot Hamam al-Hammami allegedly attacked captain Smit Machchhar and attempted to crash the aircraft. Around 180 people were on board, most of them Israelis. Machchhar, along with several Israeli passengers, managed to stop the attack and overpower al-Hammami.
flydubai seeks return to Israel
Nearly a week after the incident, Channel 13 reported on Tuesday that flydubai had sought permission to restart flights to Israel. The airline reportedly said its investigation was nearing completion and that several employees had been dismissed.
Officials from Israel’s Transportation Ministry have also reportedly been invited to visit Dubai next week. However, Transportation Minister Miri Regev has declined flydubai’s request to resume operations, according to the report.
The Transportation Ministry and Israel’s security establishment have faced criticism over their handling of foreign airline crews following the incident. Hebrew media reports on Tuesday, citing leaked comments from a closed-door meeting of the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, said about 1,240 aircrew members from hostile countries had entered Israel over the past year.
The case involving al-Hammami has drawn particular concern. He had reportedly expressed support for al-Qaeda on social media and had been prohibited from flying in Oman because of concerns about his extremist views.
Israel aims to bring stranded passengers home
The Transportation Ministry expects all Israelis stranded in Dubai after the attack to return home by Thursday, following a series of repatriation flights operated by Israeli airlines.
So far, 7,415 passengers have returned to Israel from Dubai on special flights operated by Israeli carriers, as well as from Abu Dhabi on commercial Etihad Airways flights, according to the ministry.

Michael Dell’s wife Susan Dell has made an ‘appeal’ to parents and grandparents to claim their child’s money in Trump accounts. The couple attended a press conference alongside President Donald Trump at the Oval Office celebrating the automatic enrollment of millions of American children in the ‘Trump Accounts’. “We believe in you, and we want you to dream big because we know you can make your dreams come true,” Susan 
Dell
 said adding “So parents and grandparents, please claim your child's account. These accounts are ready. They're waiting for you, and they have money in them.”
The move comes months after Michael and Susan Dell committed $6.25 billion to fund “Trump Accounts” for children in the US. Announcing the donation last year, Michael Dell said: "We've seen what happens when a child gets even a small financial headstart - their world expands".
What are Trump Accounts
Trump Accounts are new, tax-advantaged investment accounts for children in the US, created under the 2025 federal tax law known as the Working Families Tax Cuts. Legally, they are a type of traditional IRA created under new Section 530A of the tax code. Eligible US-citizen children born between January 1, 2025 and December 31, 2028 can receive a one-time $1,000 Treasury contribution, if the required election is made.
 IRS
The basic idea is to give children an investment asset early in life, allowing money to potentially grow through compound returns over many years. The Trump administration describes the programme as a way to give children a financial head start and encourage wider participation in investing.
Michael and Susan Dell donated $250 each to first 25 million Trump accounts
On July 4, as America marked its 250th birthday, the Dell Technologies founder and his wife Susan Dell gave $250 each to the first 25 million qualifying American children who sign up for a 'Trump Accounts’. Dell made the announcement on X, formerly Twitter, framing it as a "public-private partnership" that hands the next generation "a real stake in our economy." The couple had already pledged more than $6 billion to the programme back in December, so Saturday's post added a number to a commitment already made.
“Today, on America's 250th birthday, Susan and I are celebrating by giving $250 each to the first 25 million qualifying American children who sign up for their @InvestAmerica24 @TrumpAccounts. This makes every child a shareholder in the greatest prosperity-creating engine the world has ever known—American capitalism. Through this public-private partnership, we're giving the next generation a real stake in our economy and a path to the American Dream: education, a first home, starting a business, and building lasting wealth. It unites us all in hope and optimism for every child's future. Happy 250th Birthday, America!,” the post then said.

DigiKey has inaugurated a new office in Bengaluru to support its India Global Capability Center (GCC) and global business operations.
The company inaugurated the new facility on October 5, 2026, at Sumadhura Capitol Towers in Whitefield, Bengaluru. The new office is designed to support innovation, technology enablement, collaboration, and future business expansion.
“Our new Bengaluru office strengthens DigiKey’s long-term growth strategy by providing capacity to attract top talent, support business expansion and foster greater collaboration and innovation among our global team,” said Shane Zutz, Vice President of Human Resources, DigiKey.
The company said the new facility will also strengthen its ability to deliver value to customers, suppliers, and employees while expanding its access to India’s engineering talent and technology ecosystem.
DigiKey India has grown significantly since it started as a five-person prototype team in 2022. The India operation now has nearly 300 employees and serves as a strategic GCC supporting DigiKey’s global operations.
The Bengaluru center focuses on innovation, technology enablement, collaboration, and digital transformation initiatives for the company’s worldwide teams. The new office is expected to provide additional capacity as DigiKey scales its operations in India.
According to DigiKey, India has become an increasingly important market and innovation center for the company, with the Bengaluru GCC playing a key role in supporting its global technology and business requirements.
Bengaluru’s position as a major technology and innovation hub was also a factor in DigiKey’s decision to expand its presence in the city. The company said the investment will help it attract skilled professionals, improve organisational efficiency, and strengthen collaboration between its India and global teams.

articles.title: Current global crisis a testing time for Sri Lanka –Dr. Saman Weerasinghe - Daily Mirror - Sri Lanka
articles.summary: Current global crisis a testing time for Sri Lanka –Dr. Saman Weerasinghe  Daily Mirror - Sri Lanka
articles.full_text:
- The war in the Middle East has unleashed unbearable consequences for the world in terms of high fuel costs, disruption to navigation, etc.
- It is high time now for the development of new energy projects to enhance security in that perspective, as otherwise the country is susceptible to volatility in the Middle East
- To achieve long-term economic stability, Sri Lanka must urgently focus on boosting exports and expanding product diversification beyond traditional apparel and tea
Dr. Saman Weerasinghe, former Ambassador of Sri Lanka to the Russian Federation and Chairman of the board of Lay Trustees of Kelaniya Rajamaha Viharaya, shares his views Daily Mirror regarding the current global conflict situation and how Sri Lanka should navigate complexities in the advancement of its interests. Following are the excerpts of the interview -
QAs a former ambassador, how do you see the unfolding circumstances of the world? 
World history has been replete with conflicts. Power struggle has been the norm of the international order. It is natural that every country operates with the assumption that conflicts may occur at any time. What has happened now in the Middle East, Ukraine-Russia or elsewhere in the world amply describes the conflictual nature of the world. In human history, conflicts have stood in the way of progress or the realisation of the total potential of global economic development for the well-being of the entire mankind. The tools developed in the wake of World War II are not deterrent enough to prevent war. Today, the war in the Middle East has unleashed unbearable consequences for the world in terms of high fuel costs, disruption to navigation, etc. Global security is at stake. The prolonged Ukraine-Russia war is bound to trigger a food crisis. The two countries are responsible for the supply of a bulk of wheat products to the world market. The current petroleum crisis will also result in hampering fertiliser production. It is then a hit on agriculture.
I, as a former diplomat, see new security dynamics being formed as the available arrangements have failed to prevent conflicts. Saudi Arabia has teamed up with Türkiye and Pakistan, and formed the Mecca Agreement since it realised that overall reliance on the U.S. does not bode well for security in the region, as evidenced in today’s context.
QWhat does it entail for a country like Sri Lanka? 
When two elephants fight, the grass gets crushed. As such, small and medium powers such as Sri Lanka should read the scenario carefully and strategise accordingly for their security in a broader sense.
It is not only security from a military perspective, but also from energy, food, digital and other aspects. Neutrality is fundamental in the exercise of foreign policy. Yet, it is not that the current government should follow neutrality by its dictionary meaning. It is strategic, dynamic neutrality that matters in the current context.
It is high time now for the development of new energy projects to enhance security in that perspective, as otherwise the country is susceptible to volatility in the Middle East. Sri Lanka has high potential for solar and wind energy. That potential should be harnessed forthwith, and the country should advance e-mobility instead of depending on fossil fuels. It is a valuable lesson taught by the current conflicts in the world.
Again, geopolitically, it is a testing time for Sri Lanka. In a global crisis situation, the parties test who their friends or enemies are. For example, both the United States and Iran test Sri Lanka’s foreign policy. Obviously, the United States, in this instance, has more levers in prevailing upon Sri Lanka because of economic ties. Around 20 Iranian vessels that are stranded off Sri Lankan waters have reportedly sought assistance. According to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), it may require Sri Lanka to extend assistance, but practically it cannot risk American sanctions.
Sri Lanka should diversify its economy. Today, the United States is responsible for 23% of Sri Lankan exports. Overreliance on a single market is not advisable for any country in the world. It is regrettable that the present government has not prioritised trade negotiations with India and ASEAN. Also, Sri Lanka should join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) - the world’s largest free trade zone covering 15 countries, including China, Japan and Australia. If signed, it is a godsend for Sri Lanka. The need is amply felt in the current context.
To achieve long-term economic stability, Sri Lanka must urgently focus on boosting exports and expanding product diversification beyond traditional apparel and tea. Generating sustained foreign currency inflows is vital to strengthen the Sri Lankan rupee against external shocks and reduce reliance on emergency borrowing. Expanding high-value service exports such as IT, logistics, and tourism alongside higher value - added goods will directly bolster the current account balance within Sri Lanka’s Balance of Payments (BoP). A resilient current account surplus provides the ultimate shield against global energy spikes, debt pressures, and geopolitical volatility.
QSri Lanka is a strategically located country. How should Sri Lanka position itself in terms of foreign policy? 
First and foremost, Sri Lanka should read its geography properly. I wonder whether it has been done by any government or leader. In global security, geography matters more than anything. Today, despite its military might, the United States is unable to overpower Iran, which wields control over the Strait of Hormuz. It is a key chokepoint for global fuel transportation. Nearly 18 million barrels per day (bpd) pass through this strait.
Missile attacks by Yemen’s Houthi militants on maritime vessels in the Red Sea have roiled international shipping and altered the security landscape for this vital waterway connecting Africa and the Arabian Peninsula.
Sri Lanka sits along one of the world’s busiest East-West maritime shipping corridors.
Over 60 per cent of container traffic takes place through this route.
It is in close proximity to the world’s key markets like India, China and some emerging countries in the ASEAN region like Viet Nam, Thailand and Indonesia.
The country should realise the economic benefits on offer from this positioning.
Then, it is a better lever for Sri Lanka to deal with the rest of the world for its benefits.
India is critically important for Sri Lanka because of its close proximity and civilisational and cultural linkages.
While maintaining its ties with India in the proper manner, Sri Lanka should move with other countries.
China stands out as a special partner for trade and economic cooperation.
With Russia, the total potential of economic cooperation is yet to be realised.
The country should move closer to ASEAN.
Sri Lanka should further its relations with middle powers such as Australia, South Africa, Kenya, Türkiye and others.
Then, it has more space to bargain in dealing with major powers having competing interests in the world.
As a maritime nation, Sri Lanka should strengthen its naval power to protect these sea-lanes and for disaster response.
Once it is in possession of a powerful navy with air surveillance capacity, the country will have strength in the exercise of its neutrality.

QWhy has Sri Lanka been unable to realise its full potential for economic development? 
In the realisation of the fullest possible benefits from foreign relations for economic development, Sri Lanka should get its act together domestically. Lack or absence of policy consistency right throughout its post-independence history has prevented Sri Lanka from becoming a developed nation. At times, the foreign policies of the political parties remained poles apart. What one government does is completely undone by the other. Domestically, the parties can do politics, but foreign policy should not vary too widely from each other. It is important because foreign policy is no longer traditional diplomacy. It is always linked to trade, investment, technology, tourism, energy, logistics and, finally, access to global value chains. Also, Sri Lanka has so far failed to realise its areas of strength. Its relevance remains today as a maritime hub and a service hub.
Sri Lanka is blessed with an educated workforce. The International Monetary Fund has identified information technology, business-process outsourcing and tourism as sectors with potential to become important service exports. Instead of viewing these sectors separately, Sri Lanka could position itself as a regional services and connectivity hub. Sri Lanka has failed to discern its areas of strength and make proper use of its foreign policy. Domestic politics should not bar the implementation of a rightly identified foreign policy.
QHow relevant is non-aligned foreign policy in today’s context?
Non-alignment has been the trademark of Sri Lanka’s foreign policy. It is a concept developed in the wake of World War II. The developing countries took initial steps to advance their interests without being aligned with either of the two power blocs – one led by the United States of America and the other by the Soviet Union. Sri Lanka played a leading role in the Non-Aligned Movement, particularly under the leadership of Mrs Sirimavo Bandaranaike. Its conceptual meaning stays relevant even today. Today, there are multiple alliances in the world. Sri Lanka, as a country, should choose what is best for it. It is an issue-based approach. Given its positioning, it has to deal with all. India, China, Japan, the United States, Europe and Russia are equally important for Sri Lanka. Also, Sri Lanka should look at Africa as an emerging region with a lot on offer in terms of trade and investment. Accordingly, it is nothing but friendly with all, inimical with none. articles.title: When Skills Out-Earn Degrees: Is India Creating a Crisis of Education and Income? Written by Dr. Manoj Kumar Paul - Way2Barak
articles.summary: When Skills Out-Earn Degrees: Is India Creating a Crisis of Education and Income? Written by Dr. Manoj Kumar Paul  Way2Barak
articles.full_text:
For generations, Indian families followed a simple formula for their children’s future:
Study hard → obtain a degree → get a respectable job → earn a stable income → build a secure life.
That social contract is now under increasing pressure.
A young person may spend three years completing a bachelor’s degree, another two years pursuing a master’s degree, and sometimes several more years preparing for competitive examinations—only to enter the labour market at a salary lower than the monthly income of a skilled electrician, plumber, driver, technician or small trader.
The question is not whether skilled workers deserve good incomes. They absolutely do. The deeper question is:
If years of higher education, tuition fees and opportunity costs do not translate into substantially better employment opportunities, why should the next generation remain convinced that a degree is worth pursuing?
That is the education-income mismatch India cannot afford to ignore.
The provocative picture circulating on social media
The graphic accompanying this article claims that India is heading towards a “degree collapse” and that 80% of colleges could shut down within ten years. That specific figure has no authoritative evidence behind it and should not be treated as established fact.
But the underlying concern is real.
India is producing more educated young people while the economy struggles to create enough good-quality, skill-intensive jobs to absorb them.
The International Labour Organization’s India Employment Report 2024, prepared with the Institute for Human Development, describes a growing mismatch between young people’s qualifications, aspirations and available employment. Highly educated young people are increasingly accepting jobs for which they are formally overqualified.
The paradox: more education, but not necessarily a better job
In 2022, the unemployment rate among Indian youth with a graduate degree was 28.7%, compared with 3.2% among youth with less than primary education. This does not mean education causes unemployment; rather, it illustrates the difficulty educated young people can face in finding suitable employment.
The ILO also estimates that returns to education have declined over time, although graduates and postgraduates continue to have higher estimated returns than those with only secondary or higher-secondary education.
So the answer is not that “degrees are useless.”
They are not.
The economic value of a degree increasingly depends on what the degree is, where it was obtained, what skills accompany it, and whether the economy is creating jobs that require those skills.
When skills send a different economic message
Consider the everyday Indian economy.
A competent electrician can develop a loyal customer base. A plumber can charge according to urgency and expertise. A mechanic with specialised knowledge can earn well. A successful small shopkeeper can generate more income than an entry-level salaried employee.
Meanwhile, a fresh B.A., B.Com., B.Sc. or even postgraduate may enter the labour market at a modest salary.
This is not evidence that education has failed.
It shows that the labour market rewards scarcity, productivity, demand and entrepreneurship—not certificates alone.
The auto-driver versus postgraduate: A comparison!
The statement that “an auto driver earns more than a postgraduate” may certainly be true in individual cases, but it cannot be presented as a universal statistical fact.
An auto driver’s ₹30,000 may be gross receipts, from which fuel, maintenance, EMI, insurance and other expenses must be deducted. A salaried graduate may receive provident-fund contributions, paid leave, health insurance and other benefits.
Yet the comparison exposes an important reality:
A degree no longer guarantees a high starting income.
India is producing graduates faster than high-quality graduate jobs
According to the Ministry of Education’s AISHE 2021–22, higher-education enrolment reached approximately 4.33 crore students, compared with 3.42 crore in 2014–15. The country had 45,473 colleges registered with AISHE, while around 1.07 crore students passed out during that academic year.
The expansion of higher education is undoubtedly a major achievement.
But it creates another question:
Where are the corresponding jobs?
A university can produce a graduate in three years. A postgraduate can be produced in five. But high-productivity jobs cannot simply be manufactured by increasing college enrolment.
That is where the mismatch emerges.
The employability problem
The India Skills Report 2025, based on the Global Employability Test and involving more than six lakh candidates, estimated India’s graduate employability at 54.81%.
This does not mean that 45% of all Indian graduates are unemployable. The report reflects its own assessment sample and methodology.
But it highlights a serious problem:
A university degree and employability are no longer synonymous.
Employers increasingly seek communication, analytical ability, digital competence, problem-solving, adaptability, teamwork and practical experience alongside academic qualifications.
A student may know the textbook perfectly and still struggle to perform effectively in the workplace.
The real divide is no longer “degree versus no degree”
The choice should not be:
College OR skill
It should increasingly be:
College + skill + experience + adaptability
A graduate who also knows data analysis, accounting software, digital marketing, design, AI tools, communication or entrepreneurship may have a very different labour-market position from someone possessing the same degree without these capabilities.
Similarly, a student choosing an ITI, polytechnic, nursing programme, hospitality course, healthcare technology programme or other vocational pathway should not be regarded as having “failed” to enter university.
India needs both scholars and skilled technicians.
A nation cannot function without teachers, researchers, economists, engineers, doctors and administrators. But neither can it function without electricians, mechanics, machinists, plumbers, technicians, construction workers, drivers, artisans and entrepreneurs.
What the earnings data tell us
The evidence does not support the simplistic conclusion that education has stopped paying.
An IMF analysis using PLFS data from 2017–18 through 2023–24 estimates that an additional year of formal schooling in India is associated with roughly a 6–7% increase in earnings. It also finds positive returns from technical and formal training.
Formal training, according to the analysis, is associated with an earnings increase of about 18.5%, while on-the-job learning is associated with about 7.3%.
The message is therefore clear:
The future is not degree-less; it is increasingly skill-intensive.
The danger is not that young people will stop studying
The greater danger is that they will start asking:
“What exactly am I studying for?”
If a postgraduate struggles to find a ₹20,000-a-month job while a skilled technician earns considerably more, the student’s concern is understandable.
If college fees, accommodation and transportation costs are high, the return on investment in education becomes a legitimate consideration.
Education must therefore answer not merely:
“What degree will you receive?”
but also:
“What can you do with it?”
India’s demographic dividend depends on this question
India’s greatest advantage is its young population.
But a young population becomes an economic dividend only when young people are educated, skilled, employable, productively employed and adequately paid.
For India, therefore, job creation is as important as degree creation.
What should colleges do?
The answer is not to close colleges or discourage higher education. Instead, colleges must change.
1. Make every degree employability-oriented
A graduate should leave with communication skills, digital literacy, data handling and at least one marketable practical competency.
2. Make internships integral
Students should experience the workplace before graduation.
3. Bring industry into the classroom
Curricula must reflect changing workplace requirements.
4. Give vocational education social respect
There is nothing inferior about becoming an excellent electrician, technician, machinist or entrepreneur.
Skill is dignity.
5. Publish employment outcomes
Students and parents deserve to know the percentage employed, median starting salary, higher-study rate and other post-graduation outcomes.
A college should be accountable not merely for admissions and examinations, but increasingly for student outcomes.
What about the small shopkeeper?
A successful shopkeeper is not simply “someone who did not go to college.”
He or she may possess market intelligence, customer-management skills, purchasing ability, inventory management, accounting, negotiation, risk-taking ability and entrepreneurial judgement.
In other words, the shopkeeper may possess skills that formal education never certified.
The lesson is not that every graduate should abandon education and open a shop.
It is this:
The economy rewards capability, not merely certification.
We should stop asking, “Degree or skill?”
That is a false choice.
India needs a three-layer education model:
Knowledge — understanding the world.
Skill — being able to do something valuable.
Adaptability — being able to learn, change and continue learning.
The university of the future cannot simply produce degree holders.
It must produce problem-solvers.
The real “degree crisis” is a crisis of confidence
The viral graphic may exaggerate the scale of the problem, but it touches a genuine concern.
India has invested enormously in expanding higher education. With 4.33 crore students already enrolled, the question is no longer simply how to get more young people into colleges.
The harder question is:
How do we ensure that the education they receive creates economic value, social mobility and meaningful work?

articles.summary: 'No excuse for victim blaming': Mamdani under fire from Democrats and pro-Palestinian left over Oct 7 mes  The Times of IndiaFor Mamdani, Oct. 7 Anniversary Sets Off Anger and Bitterness  The New York TimesMultiple events held in New York city to mark three years of Gaza conflict  Global TimesMamdani under fire for dining at Palestinian restaurant in NYC on October 7 anniversary: ‘Making quite a statement’  Hindustan TimesAnti-Israel groups rally across US...
articles.full_text:
New York City mayor 
Zohran Mamdani
’s statement marking the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel has drawn criticism from both sides of the US political divide. Democrats and Jewish groups accusing him of shifting attention from the victims of the attack to Israel’s war in Gaza, while some on the pro-Palestinian left say he did not go far enough.
Mamdani’s statement began by calling October 7, 2023, a “profoundly painful” day and condemning Hamas’ “horrific war crimes”, including the killing of about 1,200 people in Israel and the taking of more than 250 hostages.
“We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss,” he said.
But Mamdani then turned to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, calling it a “devastating, ongoing genocide” and citing more than 74,000 deaths recorded by the Hamas-controlled Gaza health ministry.
“Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes,” Mamdani said.
He added that three years later, “occupation and apartheid continue”, while accusing the US federal government of complicity through arms shipments.
The statement drew fierce criticism from several Democratic lawmakers, who said Mamdani had made the anniversary about Israel rather than Hamas and the people killed and abducted on October 7.
Florida representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz accused Mamdani of “desecrating the memory of murdered, innocent Jews”, while New Jersey representative Josh Gottheimer said the mayor was “blaming the victims”. Jersey City mayor Steven Fulop called the statement “inappropriate and unnecessarily inflammatory”.
New York representative Dan Goldman called the message “egregious and insulting”. Goldman told Politico that October 7 should be reserved for remembering what he described as a horrific terror attack, rather than using the occasion to focus on the broader conflict.
“Regardless of what you actually think of the conflict and what’s happened either since or before, there’s no excuse for victim blaming,” Goldman said.
Brad Lander, the Mamdani-backed Democrat who defeated Goldman in this year’s primary, took a more nuanced position. He condemned Hamas but argued against forcing people to choose between mourning the victims of October 7 and acknowledging Palestinian suffering.
“We can mourn for those lost on October 7th and still acknowledge the enormous imbalance of power between Israel and the Palestinians,” Lander wrote.
Mamdani also faced criticism from Jewish organisations. Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt said the mayor’s statement did not mention Jews and accused him of using a day meant for mourning the victims of the attack to repeat his anti-Zionist arguments.
US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called the statement an “outrageous & disgusting rant”, while Ofir Akunis, Israel’s consul general in New York, called it a “disgrace, shame, and insult to the memory of those who were murdered”.
But the backlash did not come only from critics of Mamdani’s position on Israel.
Pro-Palestinian left's critique of Mamdani 
Some on the pro-Palestinian left also attacked the mayor, arguing that his stance did not go far enough. About 200 anti-Israel protesters gathered outside City Hall on Wednesday evening, with some accusing Mamdani of betraying the Palestinian cause.
Several protesters told Politico they had voted for Mamdani but would not support him for re-election because they were unhappy that he had not fired NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch, whom they described as a Zionist, or stopped some New York synagogues from hosting events promoting land sales in the occupied West Bank.
The protesters’ criticism reflected a broader frustration among some activists that Mamdani, despite his longstanding opposition to Israel’s policies, had not gone far enough in confronting Israel or supporting the Palestinian cause.
At the same time, senator Bernie Sanders, an independent who is a close adviser to Mamdani, defended the mayor’s basic framing of the conflict. Sanders said Israel had the right to defend itself and target Hamas after the October 7 attack, but accused Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government of waging “a genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza”.
Mamdani’s statement had drawn more than 11 million views on X by Wednesday evening
The controversy reflects the difficult political position Mamdani has occupied throughout his rise to power. His strong criticism of Israel helped energise young and progressive voters during his mayoral campaign, while also making him a frequent target of Jewish groups, Israeli officials and more moderate Democrats.
Mamdani has consistently rejected accusations of antisemitism, arguing that criticism of Israel and its government is distinct from hostility towards Jewish people.

articles.title: ‘Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on’: 87-year-old dies after becoming symbol of Spain housing crisis - The Times of India
articles.summary: ‘Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on’: 87-year-old dies after becoming symbol of Spain housing crisis  The Times of IndiaProtests, debate follow death of Maricarmen, 87, Spain protest symbol  Al JazeeraSpanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies  BBCEvicted Spanish octogenarian Maricarmen Abascal, heart of Spain's housing protests, has died  The HinduThousands march in Madrid after death of evicted pensioner Maricarmen  The ...
articles.full_text:
María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home triggered nationwide protests and intensified Spain’s housing crisis, died on Wednesday while in hospital.
Widely known as “Maricarmen”, Abascal had lived in the apartment for seven decades before she was evicted on September 23.
She was carried out on a stretcher after police cordoned off the street and removed protesters who had gathered to oppose the eviction. She was taken to hospital because of her fragile health.
Her death was confirmed by her lawyer Beatriz Duro and housing activists. Duro did not disclose the cause of death when confirming it to Cadena Ser radio.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez offered his condolences on social media, saying, “All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones. A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace.”
Death sparks fresh protests
News of Maricarmen’s death prompted renewed demonstrations, with protesters gathered near Spain’s Parliament chanting, “Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!”
Around 1,000 protesters had also been camping in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol over the previous week, as anger over housing costs and evictions spread across the country.
Iciar López, a 32-year-old psychologist who attended the protest in Madrid, told news agency AP, “A great deal of sorrow. And above all, the thought that she is the cause, the head of this whole revolution that has happened, and that she can’t see it. It makes me very sad that she can’t see if anything comes of it ... That’s what angers me the most, honestly.”
Maricarmen’s lawyer said the case had drawn international attention and highlighted the impact evictions can have on vulnerable people.
“Maricarmen's case, which captured media attention and traveled around the world, leaves us the image of the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the impact they can have on people’s health,” Duro said.
The Madrid Tenants’ Union said an agreement allowing Maricarmen to return to her apartment had been reached, but too late for her to go home.
“Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return home, this solution came too late,” the union said. “It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal.”
Her eviction became a national housing flashpoint
Maricarmen had spent almost her entire life in the apartment, first living there with her parents and brother. According to Spanish newspaper El País, she later worked as a secretary for the board of a pharmaceutical company. She said both her parents died in the apartment.
After retiring in 1998, she spent much of her time walking around the neighbourhood, running errands and looking after her belongings at home. Family photographs were among the few possessions she had taken with her to hospital.
The real estate company that evicted her had sought to rent the property at a much higher price. After sustained public pressure, it eventually agreed to let her return.
Her case became a rallying point for renters facing rising housing costs. Protesters across Spain have carried slogans including “Not even one more Maricarmen!” while demanding action from lawmakers.
Eugenio Melchor, 22, who attended Wednesday’s protest in Madrid, said: “Maricarmen only wanted to die in her home.
She wasn’t asking for anything else. She was dying in her home and she almost did. They have killed her. I mean, there’s no other word for it, and I hope those responsible for this pay and go to trial.”
Housing crisis deepens political pressure
Spain’s housing problems have been building for years, with renters increasingly protesting over rising costs and the limited supply of rental homes.
The average rent in Spain has almost doubled over the past decade, according to property website Idealista, with the price per square metre rising from 8.20 euros in 2016 to 15.10 euros this year.
Spain’s government said 26% of renters spend an average of 40% of their income on rent and utilities, compared with 18% across the European Union. Government-owned rental properties account for less than 2% of Spain’s available housing stock, compared with an EU average of 8%.
The protests have also shaken Spanish politics. Sánchez called an early election after his government failed to secure parliamentary backing for emergency housing measures aimed at stopping evictions and curbing real estate speculation. The election is scheduled for November 29.
Housing minister Isabel Rodríguez also expressed her condolences, writing, “I deeply lament the death of Maricarmen. My condolences to those who accompanied her and fought by her side until the end.”
Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also offered condolences, saying, “I want to express my condolences to Maricarmen's family and loved ones. No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage. When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect.”

articles.title: US visa curbs may shift higher-value tech work to India says former HCL Tech CEO Vineet Nayar - Times of Oman
articles.summary: US visa curbs may shift higher-value tech work to India says former HCL Tech CEO Vineet Nayar  Times of Oman
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: US restrictions on Indian technology professionals could encourage American companies to shift more high-value technology work to India, including artificial intelligence (AI), product engineering and cybersecurity, former HCL Technologies CEO Vineet Nayar said.
In a post on X, Nayar said the US move to restrict several major technology companies from using the Permanent Labour Certification Program (PERM) could have an unintended impact by accelerating the transfer of technology work to India.
“America is making it harder to move Indian talent there, while technology is making it easier for smaller teams in India to take responsibility for increasingly sophisticated work,” Nayar said.
He noted that Indian IT companies accounted for fewer than 1,400 of the 117,849 PERM certifications issued last year, representing less than 2 per cent of the total. This, he said, suggests that the direct impact on Indian IT firms could be limited.
Nayar said the Indian IT industry could be entering a new phase, moving beyond its traditional model of sending engineers to client locations in the US and gradually shifting work to India.
The next stage, he said, could see Indian teams taking greater responsibility for designing and developing technology, rather than simply executing instructions from overseas clients.
“The opportunity is architecture, product engineering, cybersecurity, AI implementation, industry solutions and eventually ownership of products and IP,” he said.
The remarks come after the US government announced restrictions on several major technology and outsourcing companies, including Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Infosys, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Cognizant, under the PERM programme amid investigations into alleged misuse of the system. US technology companies Microsoft and Adobe were also named in the action.
US Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling said the companies had collectively sought millions of foreign workers and received hundreds of thousands of H-1B visa approvals and permanent labour certifications. He said the action was aimed at addressing concerns over foreign hiring and protecting American workers.
TCS said it would comply with any directive issued by the US Department of Labour, adding that its workforce strategy in the country was based on local hiring.
The company said its PERM applications had remained in single digits over the previous two years and that it did not expect the suspension to affect its workforce strategy or customer engagements. TCS also reiterated its plan to hire an additional 15,000 employees in the US over five years.
Nayar also cautioned that artificial intelligence could weaken the traditional relationship between business growth and employment in the Indian IT sector.
“For thirty years, Indian IT competed largely on the cost of Indian talent. The next thirty will depend on the capability of Indian talent,” he said.
He added that the industry's future growth would depend on its ability to develop products, build a larger pool of technology architects and shift more global technology decision-making to India.
This could help Indian IT companies generate greater value per employee, even if employment growth does not keep pace with business expansion.

articles.title: 8 IT firms including TCS, Infosys suspended from US green card programme: How does it hit Indian professi - The Times of India
articles.summary: 8 IT firms including TCS, Infosys suspended from US green card programme: How does it hit Indian professi  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
In yet another blow to the Indian IT sector and its professionals, the Donald Trump administration has barred as many as eight technology companies from participating in a programme that is used to seek green cards for foreign workers. The move has the potential to affect tens of thousands of India’s IT professionals.
The list of companies which have been suspended from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme (PERM) includes IT sector majors like 
TCS
, 
Infosys
, Microsoft, Wipro, and Cognizant. Indian professionals account for more than 70% of H-1B petitions approved each year.
India accounts for a large share of H-1B beneficiaries. As a result, the recent developments could potentially have a significant impact on Indian technology professionals and engineers working in the United States.
Also Read | 
‘Death by restriction’: As Trump sours H-1B visa dream, which Indian IT professionals face the biggest hit?
What is PERM?
PERM essentially acts as a bridge between being a temporary foreign worker in the US and a realistic pathway to permanent residency in America.
It is a crucial stage in the process of getting employment-based green cards in the US. An employer requires certification from the Department of Labour (DoL) that confirms that no willing and qualified US workers are available for that position, before they are allowed to sponsor the green card of a foreign worker. 
The certification must also establish that employing the foreign national will not adversely affect wages or working conditions in the US.
What it PERM?
These eight firms have been suspended from that programme, effectively putting a halt to their ability to offer employment-based green cards to their employees.
It does not, however, revoke H-1B visas or immediately stop the companies concerned from employing foreign nationals.
US immigration rules allow certain H-1B workers to extend their stay beyond the standard six-year limit once they have reached specified stages of the employment-based green-card process.
The companies affected by the decision have the option of challenging it before a federal court.
What has been announced?
The step was announced by US Vice President J D Vance, Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling and Attorney General Todd Blanche under the US Anti-Fraud Task Force initiative.
"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," Sonderling said.
He added that the Department of Labour was also suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the programme because both companies are facing multiple active federal investigations.
US Suspends 8 IT Firms From PERM
Vance alleged that Microsoft has laid off 6,000 American workers in 2025, certifying that it could not find US workers who were suitably qualified for the jobs. Yet, Microsoft has got the approval for over 6,000 H-1B visas. It also submitted over 3,600 applications for permanent labour certification.
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
The Department of Labour will now stop accepting fresh applications from the companies and would not process any of their permanent labour certification applications that were already pending.
“Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications,” Sonderling said.
He claimed that the numbers represented hundreds of thousands of employment opportunities taken away from American workers.
Vance described foreign employees recruited through H-1B visas as “foreign indentured servants” and labelled companies that rely on the programme as “visa mills”.
Why has Trump administration taken this step?
The move comes after allegations that the PERM system has prevented Americans from getting jobs.
According to Rajiv Dabhadkar, Founder, National Organization For Software and Technology Professionals, the most important message here is that Washington is no longer looking only at whether an H-1B worker is legally qualified. It is increasingly questioning the business model through which foreign labour is recruited, deployed and paid.
“The US administration's stated concern is that some employers and body shops may have used foreign workers in ways that disadvantage American workers, through wage suppression and other forms of programme abuse. These allegations need to be investigated on their merits. Hence it is not about Indian professionals being treated as the problem. The focus is on employers and intermediaries that may have exploited the system,” he tells TOI.
Rajiv Dabhadkar explains with an example:
Suppose, a US company pays $150,000 for a technology position. An intermediary recruits an H-1B worker and constructs an employment chain where the worker receives substantially less than the economic value of the position. The difference becomes the intermediary's margin.
If a similarly qualified American worker would cost more, the employer may have an economic incentive to use the intermediary. In that situation, the real problem is not: Indian worker vs American worker.
It is: transparent market wage vs labour arbitrage.
“That is why the current federal investigation into employers, staffing companies and labor brokers is potentially more consequential than the headline debate,” Dabhadkar explains.
What is the impact on Indian IT professionals?
Indian IT sector companies and thousands of IT professionals now face multiple uncertainties. Every route to securing a job and permanent residency in the US is becoming tougher.
A $70,000 fee to get a job after you do education in the US, a proposed $100,000 H-1B visa fee, and now the suspension of major technology firms from PERM all add up to a difficult scenario.
Top 10 countries of birth of approved H-1B visas
By suspending major IT companies from the PERM programme, the US government is effectively putting another barrier in front of thousands of Indian professionals who may already have spent years working, paying taxes and building careers in the United States.
The important thing to understand is that the PERM move does not by itself affect the validity of H-1B status for employees who are already in the United States.
“But, it could have a more significant impact on H-1B workers who are approaching the six-year limit and are dependent on the PERM-based employment Green Card process to extend their stay in the United States,” says Kuldip Kumar, Partner at Mainstay Tax Advisors LLP.
Separately, the Trump administration's earlier $100,000 payment requirement in relation to certain new H-1B petitions has also been extended through September 21, 2027. However, the implementation of the fee is currently blocked by federal court orders while the litigation continues.
“Taken together, these developments reflect the Trump administration's stated focus on protecting US workers and increasing scrutiny of programmes that allow US employers to hire and retain foreign workers,” Kuldip Kumar tells TOI.
“The longer-term impact on Indian technology professionals, particularly those dependent on the H-1B-to-Green Card pathway, will depend significantly on how these measures are ultimately implemented and how long they remain in effect,” he adds.
H-1B visas: Top employers
Xiao Wang, CEO of Boundless Immigration breaks down the impact into two categories of Indian IT professionals:
Those already in the US at a suspended firm:
 H-1B status is fine for now. The problem is for anyone counting on their employer to start the green card process.
“PERM is step one, and if TCS, Wipro, Infosys, HCL, or Cognizant can't file new applications, those workers' green card clocks don't start. For someone near the six-year H-1B limit without an approved I-140, this is serious and employees need to find new jobs if they want more confidence around being able to stay in the US long-term,” Wang tells TOI.
IT professionals looking to come to the US through these firms:
 The path just got harder! These companies have historically been the biggest H-1B sponsors for workers coming from India.
“With PERM suspended and H-1B registrations already down sharply, the traditional IT consulting pipeline is effectively frozen to the US,” Wang warns.
The biggest takeaway, however, is that this move is not an isolated step or a temporary blip.
“The DOL suspension, combined with the $100,000 H-1B fee and the wage-weighted lottery, is systematically dismantling the staffing model that brought hundreds of thousands of Indian engineers to the US over 30 years,” Wang says.
He believes that senior engineers at US tech firms are largely insulated.
”Early-career and mid-level professionals at the Indian IT consulting firms are the ones getting squeezed,” he notes.

VIJAYAWADA: Advocating a transformative water-security roadmap for South India, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu urged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to prioritise the strategic Godavari–Cauvery river interlinking project to permanently resolve water scarcity across Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.
Meeting the Prime Minister in New Delhi on Thursday evening, Naidu congratulated Modi on completing 25 years in public life, commending his visionary leadership, decisive governance, and unwavering commitment to cooperative federalism in empowering States as equal partners toward achieving a ‘Viksit Bharat’.
Proposing the creation of a national ‘Water Grid’ through large-scale river interlinking—drawing a direct parallel with nationwide highway networks and unified power grids built under NDA administrations—Naidu submitted a detailed status report on the Polavaram Irrigation Project. He also requested Central financial assistance for the upcoming Godavari Pushkarams in 2027, which is expected to attract millions of pilgrims.
Addressing agrarian concerns, Naidu informed Modi that El Niño conditions had triggered a severe 53% rainfall deficit in AP.
CM holds talks with Shah on pending State issues; seeks saline land transfer
He detailed the State’s ongoing drought mitigation measures alongside recent agricultural milestones, including the launch of the Global Horticulture Hub at Madanapalle with Central cooperation, and the foundation stone laying for an Indian School of Agriculture, planned on the lines of ISB.
He also sought the Centre’s support for major infrastructure projects in AP, including the proposed Outer Ring Road in the capital Amaravati, approval for the Visakhapatnam Metro, and briefed the Prime Minister on the proposed Beach Road project.
