Naidu also pressed for Central cooperation to construct the Visakhapatnam Beach Road project to connect coastal industrial hubs, ports, and tourism centres, and requested federal backing for an iconic bridge at the Polavaram project site connecting the left and right flanks, along with associated feeder roads and bridges.
Focusing on port-led industrial expansion, Naidu met Union Minister for Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal, requesting the transfer of 20,378 acres of saline lands currently under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) to the State government.
Naidu explained that these lands are crucial for establishing port-based industrial zones, road and rail connectivity, and logistics infrastructure. Furthermore, he sought the Commerce Ministry’s support to strengthen international market linkages, processing facilities, quality standards, and export infrastructure for AP’s commercial crops, including chilli, tobacco, and aqua products.

articles.title: What Trump’s PERM crackdown could mean for Indian tech workers and IT firms - DQ
articles.summary: What Trump’s PERM crackdown could mean for Indian tech workers and IT firms  DQ
articles.full_text:
The Trump administration's decision to suspend eight major technology companies from a key US green-card process has reopened a contentious debate over foreign workers, immigration practices, and the future of India's IT services industry.
Announced on October 8, 2026, the suspension covers Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCLTech, and Capgemini. The US Department of Labor has said it will neither accept new applications nor process pending cases involving these employers under the Permanent Labor Certification programme, commonly known as PERM.
US Vice-President JD Vance criticised Microsoft's reliance on foreign workers while laying off American employees. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling went further, claiming that the eight companies had collectively sought nearly three million foreign workers, obtained over 230,000 H-1B approvals, and received more than 100,000 permanent labour certifications since 2009.
These are the administration's figures, not evidence that an equivalent number of American jobs was lost. Visa approvals can include extensions for existing employees, a distinction Microsoft has emphasised in its response.
For Indian professionals, however, the immediate concern is more personal. What happens to a green-card application already caught in America's lengthy immigration queue? And what if an H-1B visa is approaching its expiry?
What is PERM, and why does it matter?
PERM is the electronic system used to administer permanent labour certification, a crucial step in many employment-based green-card applications.
Before sponsoring a foreign employee for permanent residence, an employer generally must establish that qualified and available American workers cannot be found for the position and that hiring the foreign worker will not adversely affect local wages and working conditions.
Once certified, the employer usually files Form I-140, the Immigrant Petition for Alien Workers, with US Citizenship and Immigration Services. The employee then waits until an immigrant visa number becomes available before completing the permanent-residence process.
The H-1B programme is different. It allows employers to hire foreign professionals temporarily in specialised occupations. Suspending PERM applications does not automatically cancel an employee's existing H-1B status.
But it can interrupt the transition from temporary employment to permanent residence.
Why these companies, and has fraud been established?
The administration alleges that immigration programmes have been misused to favour foreign workers, potentially displacing Americans or undercutting wages.
Yet an investigation is not a finding of guilt.
Under existing US regulations, authorities can suspend permanent labour certification processing during investigations into possible fraud or wilful misrepresentation. An initial suspension may last up to 180 days, with provisions for extensions.
The government has not publicly established that all eight companies committed the alleged violations. The inclusion of Microsoft and Adobe also shows that the action extends beyond Indian outsourcing companies.
There is a legitimate policy question beneath the political rhetoric: are employers genuinely testing the American labour market, or using recruitment procedures that make hiring foreign workers easier?
The timing, ahead of the US midterm elections, gives the announcement an unmistakable political dimension. But the enforcement powers themselves predate the Trump administration.
Has the immigration system been abused before?
There is documented evidence of immigration-related violations and disputed recruitment practices, involving Indian services companies as well as American technology businesses.
In 2013, Infosys agreed to pay USD 34 million to settle US government allegations involving visa practices, including the use of B-1 business visas and H-1B procedures. The agreement included enhanced compliance measures. Infosys said the civil settlement involved no criminal charges or court rulings against the company.
In 2021, Facebook reached settlements with US authorities over recruitment practices connected with PERM. The Justice Department alleged that the company had discouraged American applicants from seeking positions intended for temporary visa holders. Facebook agreed to a USD 4.75 million civil penalty and a back-pay fund of up to USD 9.5 million.
These cases demonstrate that immigration enforcement concerns are not imaginary. But historical settlements cannot establish wrongdoing in the current investigations.
The more important question is whether the authorities can substantiate the allegations against each suspended employer.
India's green-card backlog was already severe
For Indians, the latest suspension adds uncertainty to a long-standing problem.
The October 2026 US Visa Bulletin lists November 1, 2013 as the final-action date for Indian applicants under Employment-Based Second Preference (EB-2), covering advanced-degree professionals and people of exceptional ability.
For Employment-Based Third Preference (EB-3), which includes skilled workers and professionals, the corresponding date is January 1, 2014.
For most other countries, the respective dates are January 1, 2025 and May 15, 2024.
These are priority-date cut-offs, not precise predictions of individual waiting periods. Nevertheless, they illustrate India's substantial backlog.
The PERM suspension creates another difficulty for workers who have not completed the labour-certification stage.
Those with approved immigrant petitions are in a different position. Their existing approvals and priority dates are not automatically invalidated by the suspension.
What if an H-1B visa is about to expire?
The greatest immediate uncertainty may concern employees approaching the normal six-year limit on H-1B status.
US immigration rules permit extensions beyond six years in certain circumstances. For example, qualifying workers may receive one-year extensions when a labour certification or immigrant petition was filed at least 365 days before the extended period begins.
Workers with approved immigrant petitions who cannot obtain permanent residence because immigrant visas are unavailable may qualify for extensions of up to three years.
But an employee whose employer has not yet filed PERM could face difficulties establishing eligibility for such extensions.
There is also a distinction between an expired visa stamp and an expiring period of authorised stay. They do not necessarily occur together.
The suspension does not automatically prevent otherwise eligible H-1B extensions. Employees should therefore assess their specific circumstances rather than assume their ability to remain in the US has ended.
For families, these distinctions affect decisions about employment, housing, education, and long-term settlement.
Nasscom argues the immediate impact may be limited
India's technology industry has sought to distinguish temporary skilled-worker mobility from permanent immigration.
Responding to the suspension, Nasscom said Indian technology companies had substantially reduced their dependence on H-1B visas while expanding local hiring in the US.
It also maintained that relatively few employees transition from H-1B status to permanent residence through PERM.
That suggests the immediate operational impact on Indian IT services companies could be narrower than the announcement implies.
However, a limited number of affected employees does not make their individual circumstances insignificant. More broadly, uncertainty over immigration policy can complicate long-term workforce planning.
How dependent is Indian IT on America?
The commercial relationship with the US remains central to India's IT services industry.
FY2025–26 disclosures show TCS generated approximately 50.6% of revenue from the Americas, Infosys 56.1% from North America, HCLTech 55.5% from the US, Wipro 62.4% through its two Americas market units, and Tech Mahindra 49.8% from the Americas.
These geographical classifications differ and cannot be treated as identical US-only figures. Nor do they measure dependence on H-1B employees.
Nevertheless, they demonstrate the industry's considerable exposure to American enterprise spending.
Diversification is an obvious response, but Europe is not a straightforward substitute. Its slower economic growth, regulatory requirements, and cautious enterprise spending present different challenges.
Opportunities exist in cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, regulated technology services, and enterprise modernisation. But expanding in Europe demands more than transferring the American outsourcing model to another geography.
Is this a fundamental reset for Indian IT services?
The PERM suspension alone is unlikely to overturn the Indian IT services model. Companies have already expanded offshore delivery, local recruitment, and specialised consulting.
But the industry faces several pressures simultaneously: immigration restrictions, changing customer expectations, rising compliance costs, and automation reducing the effort required for some traditional software and support activities.
It is to be seen, whether future growth can continue to depend so heavily on large workforces, American customers, and the flexibility to move professionals across borders.
Indian IT services companies may need to strengthen local delivery capabilities, diversify customer markets, and increasingly charge for business results rather than the number of engineers assigned to projects.
None of this suggests that the US market will become less important. Its scale makes that unlikely in the foreseeable future.
The immediate outcome of the PERM investigations remains uncertain. The wider industry challenge, however, is already visible.
For decades, Indian IT services succeeded by connecting India's engineering talent with global technology demand. Its next phase may depend less on moving people

Kolkata: The Donald Trump government has suspended eight IT companies, including Microsoft, Tata, Infosys, and Wipro, from a program that allows foreign workers to apply for green cards. They argued that this practice is pushing American citizens out of the job market. Following the Trump administration’s decision, American Depository Receipts (ADRs) of Indian IT companies Infosys and Wipro fell by about 3%. Needless to mention, the shares of all IT majors such as TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Tech Mahindra, HCL Tech will be in focus as trading begins shortly in the Indian market.
Firms left out of the H-1B visa program
This decline came after US President Donald Trump’s administration suspended these companies from the ‘Permanent Labor Certification Program’. Under this program, companies can apply for green cards for employees with H-1B visas. Apart from Infosys and Wipro, other Indian tech companies like Tata and HCL Tech, and US companies with a large presence in India – such as Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe – were also included in the list.
What is an ADR?
American Depository Receipts (ADRs) are a significant financial instrument for Indian IT companies. They allow investments in Indian company shares on the US stock market. To raise money from US investors, Indian companies can issue ADRs in the US market. US investors buy and sell these ADRs in dollars. Each ADR can represent one or more common shares of the company.
ADRs are important for mobilising foreign investment and gain global recognition. Moreover, fluctuations in the price of ADRs can also impact the company’s Indian shares, though both markets may not always move in the same direction.
Indian IT sector’s US earnings
According to reports, India’s $300 billion IT sector earns as much as 57% of its revenue from the US. The entire IT industry has long benefited from the US work visa program and outsourcing of software and business services. In recent years, tech companies have reduced their reliance on H-1B visas by hiring locally and ‘nearshoring’ (outsourcing work to nearby countries).
Last year, approximately 57,000 new H-1B visas were approved for Indians, a 28% decrease over FY24. In September of last year, the US increased the H-1B visa fee for new applicants to $100,000 annually.
Action under the US Anti-Fraud Task Force
The exclusion of these companies from the Green Card program was announced by US vice president J D Vance, labour secretary Keith Sonderling and attorney general Todd Blanco as part of an action taken by the US Anti-Fraud Task Force. “I am suspending some of the world’s largest IT outsourcing companies – Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini – from the Permanent Labor Certification Program,” said Sonderling. He added the Labour Department is also suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the program due to several active federal investigations.
“Since 2009, these companies alone have sought nearly 3 million foreign workers. They have received more than 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and more than 100,000 Permanent Labor Certifications,” Sonderling said.

articles.full_text:
A number of casualties have been reported after a tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency has announced.
The vessel was hit by several projectiles 94 kilometres (58 miles) north of Madinat ash Shamal, UKMTO said on Wednesday. The incident comes as the British maritime agency reported a recent rise in attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
UKMTO did not say how many people were killed or injured in this latest attack, adding that authorities were investigating. It did not specify the origin of the ship.
An attack on a vessel in the middle of the Gulf is unusual. The Maritime Executive, a publication specialising in commercial shipping, said it was the first reported attack on a tanker in the western half of the Gulf in weeks.
Qatar has not commented on the reported attack, which falls within its exclusive economic zone.
Vessels have more commonly been targeted in the strategically important Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway linking the Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.
Before the United States-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the strait typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day, and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies.
In retaliation for US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait, while Washington has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports.
UKMTO said on Tuesday that there had been nine attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and the Gulf combined.
Despite the attacks, oil exports from the Middle East have risen to, and according to provisional data even surpassed, pre-war levels in recent weeks.
The seven-day moving average of Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with about 18 million bpd on average in the 12 months before the war, according to Kpler, a data firm.
